accuracy.evidence: Forms checked against Cambridge Grammar of English and the Oxford Learner's grammar pages on comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs: one-syllable -er/-est with drop-e and consonant doubling (big, bigger), two-syllable -y words to -ier/-iest (happier), more/most for careful, famous, beautiful, dangerous, exciting; irregulars good/better/best, bad/worse/worst, many/more/most, far/further/furthest; -ly adverbs with more/most (more carefully, most loudly), flat adverbs fast/faster and hard/harder, well/better. little was deliberately left out of the rule-breaker rows because littlest is a real size form. The adult text notes the two-syllable words that take either form (clever, quiet).

misconceptions.evidence: Each documented slip has a step: double marking (step 5 deletes more in more taller, most in most biggest, more in more better; challenge 'double'), regularised irregulars (step 3 gooder, baddest, manier, goodest, farest; challenge 'irreg'), -er on long words (step 2 prediction beautifuller; challenge 'long'), more on short words (step 4 more fast, more hard; challenge 'short'), superlative for two (step 1 two-tower rounds reject tallest; challenge 'group'), y-to-i and doubling spelling (challenge 'yrule', 'spell').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagcmpsup is built around this topic's own decision: how many things are compared (two drawn towers versus three, with the target tower outlined) and how long the word is (syllable count shown under each card decides -er or more), then the irregular three-column table and deleting the second marker in double comparisons. The suffix lab flagsfxrule practises spelling rules for many suffixes and the adjective/adverb lab flagadjadv picks word class; neither compares quantities or counts syllables to choose more. lab_distinct passed under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers the two-versus-many rule from the pictures: putting tallest into the two-tower sentence returns 'Only two towers, so compare them with -er and than: taller.' Dropping beautiful into the -er box returns 'beautiful has 3 syllables. Long words take more: more beautiful, not beautifuler.' Tapping more in Sam is more taller than me returns 'taller already compares, so more goes.' The done screens restate the rules with the learner's own answers.

predictions.evidence: Two predictions each hold a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'taller' for the highest of three towers (step 1 rounds 2, 4 and 5 need the -est form), and 'beautifuller' as the comparative of beautiful (step 2 sorts it into more). The third, 'more fast' versus 'faster', is disproved by the first adverb sentence in step 4.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with nine distinct wrong-answer messages: group (two racers need -er and than), double (compares twice), long (3 syllables so more), irreg (good, better, best), spell (double the g in bigger), short (big takes -er), yrule (y to i in happiest), pair (a whole class needs the and -est), ly (slowly takes more).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and concrete examples (A giraffe is taller than a horse; Say beautiful. It has three beats.). The adult text was rewritten from FK grade 11.1 into shorter sentences after the first readability check; validate_lessons now passes for kid and adult text. Lab banners stay short ('Word 1 of 8: clap it, then choose').

no_filler.evidence: Each kid sentence carries a rule or an example; adult paragraphs give the curriculum place, the syllable rule with spelling changes, the irregulars, the adverb rule and a list of named mistakes, then what each lab step does. The content gate found no filler phrases and less than 12% overlap with any other lesson, including Adjectives and adverbs and Suffixes.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 x 640 screenshots in light and dark themes for every step: the towers, word cards and the three-column rule-breaker row fit without clipping, two sorting boxes sit side by side with readable 14 px labels, the six-word double-comparison sentence wraps onto two rows, and the button pad below wraps. The browser gate also passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button twin (Fill the gap with taller, cold: add -er / -est, Delete more); the canvas aria-label is updated with each feedback line; the challenge uses buttons and a role=status live region; axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme on desktop and iPhone 13.
